how_to_obtain.expected_output: PowerShell returns 'Value: 30000000' (default ~28.6 MB). The value in bytes is the enforced limit.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test empirically by attempting an oversized POST and observing the response code (413 = limit enforced, 200/500 = no limit or limit not enforced).
how_to_obtain.command: dd if=/dev/urandom bs=1M count=50 2>/dev/null | curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/octet-stream' --data-binary @- http://localhost/
how_to_obtain.expected_output: HTTP 413 (Request Entity Too Large) confirms a body size limit is enforced. HTTP 200 or 500 suggests no effective limit at the server layer.

option_description: Indicates whether the web server is serving its vendor-default welcome or index page (e.g., Apache 'It works!', nginx default page, IIS default welcome page) on the root path or well-known paths, typically indicating the server has not been fully configured for production use.
security_impact: Directly triggers the default_or_sample_content_present Rego rule when true. The presence of a default welcome page confirms the server software identity and version to unauthenticated clients (T1082 System Information Discovery, T1592.002 Software), assisting targeted exploit selection. It also signals the server may be in an unconfigured or lightly hardened state, making additional default content or credential exposure (T1078.001 Default Accounts) more likely. Combined with version_has_known_cve, it creates a high-confidence exploitation scenario.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Send an HTTP GET request to the server root and check the response body for known default page markers.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s http://localhost/ | grep -iE 'It works!|Welcome to nginx|nginx default|IIS Windows Server|Test Page for|Apache HTTP Server|noindex\.html'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: String matches like 'Welcome to nginx!' or 'It works!' in the response body confirm the default welcome page is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test both HTTP and HTTPS and check the HTTP status and content length to distinguish a real application response from a default page.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sIL http://localhost/ ; curl -sIL https://localhost/ -k ; curl -s http://localhost/ | wc -c
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A small response body (typically < 5 KB) with HTTP 200 and matching default page text strongly suggests the default page is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether the server's document root contains only the vendor-default index file and no application content.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Only 'index.html' or 'index.nginx-debian.html' present with no application files indicates the default content has not been replaced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Open a browser and navigate to the server's IP or hostname on port 80 and 443 to visually confirm the presence of a default vendor welcome page.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Navigate to http://<server-ip>/ and https://<server-ip>/. A rendered default page (nginx blue/white, Apache orange test page, IIS splash screen) visually confirms the attribute is true.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Vendor-branded welcome page rendered in the browser without any application-specific branding or content.

option_description: Indicates whether vendor-shipped sample scripts, test pages, demonstration endpoints, or diagnostic pages included with the web server package are reachable via HTTP and return a 2xx or 3xx response, indicating they have not been removed or blocked post-installation.
security_impact: Directly triggers the default_or_sample_content_present Rego rule when true. Sample scripts and test endpoints (e.g., /phpinfo.php, /examples/, /cgi-bin/test-cgi, Tomcat /manager/) expose detailed server configuration, environment variables, PHP build flags, and loaded modules (T1592.002 Software). Many have historically contained exploitable vulnerabilities themselves (T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application). Tomcat /manager/ may expose default credentials (T1078.001). phpinfo.php discloses file paths, session configurations, and extension versions that directly inform exploitation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Probe known vendor sample paths using curl and check HTTP response codes for accessibility.
how_to_obtain.command: for path in /phpinfo.php /info.php /test.php /examples/ /manager/ /host-manager/ /cgi-bin/test-cgi /manual/ /server-info /server-status /iisstart.htm /.well-known/security.txt; do code=$(curl -o /dev/null -sk -w '%{http_code}' http://localhost${path}); echo "$code $path"; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any path returning HTTP 200, 301, or 302 indicates the sample content is accessible. HTTP 403 or 404 indicates it has been blocked or removed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test HTTPS equivalents of the same paths and also probe for Tomcat management interfaces on alternative ports.
how_to_obtain.command: for path in /examples/servlets/ /examples/jsp/ /manager/html /host-manager/html; do code=$(curl -o /dev/null -sk -w '%{http_code}' https://localhost${path}); echo "$code $path"; done ; curl -so /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://localhost:8080/manager/html
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Tomcat manager returning 200 or 401 (authentication prompt) indicates the management interface is exposed. JSP/servlet examples returning 200 confirms sample content accessibility.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the filesystem for sample scripts and test pages that are present in the document root or CGI directories.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Finding any of these files indicates they exist on disk. Presence alone does not confirm accessibility; combine with network test to confirm HTTP reachability.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Apache, verify whether /server-status and /server-info handlers are enabled and accessible without IP restriction.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'server-status\|server-info\|ExtendedStatus' /etc/apache2/ /etc/httpd/ 2>/dev/null ; curl -s http://localhost/server-status?auto | head -5 ; curl -s http://localhost/server-info | head -5
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A non-empty response from /server-status?auto (showing 'Total Accesses:' etc.) or /server-info (showing module list) confirms the diagnostic endpoint is publicly accessible.

option_description: Controls whether two or more virtual hosts are configured to resolve to the identical filesystem document root directory. When multiple vhosts point to the same root, a request authenticated or routed to one vhost can access files intended exclusively for another, collapsing intended content isolation boundaries.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the `misconfigured_virtual_host_isolation` exposure directly when `input.vhosts_share_document_root == true`. This enables cross-vhost content access (MITRE T1611 Escape to Host, T1090.004 Domain Fronting), allowing an attacker targeting a lower-trust vhost to read or serve files belonging to a higher-trust vhost on the same server, potentially including configuration files, credentials, or application source.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract all DocumentRoot values from Apache configuration and check for duplicates using grep and sort. Run against the live merged configuration to catch includes.
how_to_obtain.command: apachectl -S 2>&1 | grep -i 'document root' ; grep -rih 'DocumentRoot' /etc/apache2/ /etc/httpd/ 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $2}' | sort | uniq -d
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If any path appears more than once in the output of `uniq -d`, vhosts_share_document_root should be set to true. No output means all roots are unique.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For nginx, extract all `root` directives from server blocks and identify duplicates, resolving symlinks to compare canonical paths.
how_to_obtain.command: nginx -T 2>/dev/null | grep -E '^\s*(root|server_name)' | awk '/server_name/{name=$2} /root/{print $2, name}' | sort | awk '{print $1}' | uniq -d
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any root path printed by `uniq -d` confirms shared document roots across server blocks; true should be returned.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Manually inspect each VirtualHost block in Apache or server block in nginx, resolve any relative paths or symlinks with `realpath`, and compare the canonical absolute paths side by side.
how_to_obtain.command: for d in $(grep -rih 'DocumentRoot' /etc/apache2/ /etc/httpd/ 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $2}'); do realpath "$d" 2>/dev/null; done | sort | uniq -d
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Duplicate canonical paths confirm shared document roots. Empty output means roots are distinct.

typical_values: true (shared root, common in default/single-site setups misapplied to multi-tenant configs)

option_description: Indicates whether each virtual host's process or worker operates inside a chroot jail, Linux namespace, container boundary, or equivalent OS-level isolation mechanism that restricts filesystem traversal to only that vhost's intended directory tree, preventing one compromised vhost from reaching another vhost's files.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers `misconfigured_virtual_host_isolation` when both `chroot_or_namespace_isolation_enabled` is false AND `path_traversal_controls_enabled` is false. Without this isolation layer, a path traversal or LFI vulnerability in any hosted application can reach files across all vhost roots and system directories. This directly enables T1611 (Escape to Host) and complements traversal-based attacks. The absence of isolation maximises blast radius for any single-vhost compromise.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether the Apache ChrootDir directive is present and active in the server configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A non-empty result with a valid directory path confirms chroot is configured. No output means chroot is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the systemd service unit for the web server to check for RootDirectory= or PrivateTmp= isolation settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: RootDirectory=/some/chroot/path or PrivateTmp=yes confirms OS-level isolation. Missing entries indicate no systemd isolation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Determine if the web server worker processes are running inside a container namespace by inspecting their namespace links.
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep -E 'apache2|nginx|httpd' | grep -v grep | awk '{print $2}' | head -5 | xargs -I{} ls -la /proc/{}/ns/ 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Namespace inodes differing from the host PID 1 namespace (compare with `ls -la /proc/1/ns/`) indicate container or namespace isolation. Matching inodes mean no namespace isolation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review nginx configuration for chroot wrapper scripts or OS-level jail configuration files (e.g., FreeBSD jail.conf, firejail profiles).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Relevant configuration entries referencing chroot paths or jail names confirm isolation is configured.

typical_values: false (most default OS package installations have no chroot or namespace isolation)
true (hardened deployments using systemd RootDirectory=, Docker containers, or explicit ChrootDir directives)

option_description: Indicates whether the server configuration actively prevents directory traversal sequences (sequences such as `../` or URL-encoded equivalents) from resolving to filesystem paths outside the intended document root for each virtual host. Controls include disabling FollowSymLinks, enabling `disable_symlinks on` in nginx, and absence of rewrite rules that permit out-of-root resolution.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `misconfigured_virtual_host_isolation` when both `path_traversal_controls_enabled` is false AND `chroot_or_namespace_isolation_enabled` is false. Without traversal controls, an attacker can craft requests such as `GET /../../../../etc/passwd` to read arbitrary system files, enabling credential theft and reconnaissance. This directly supports T1611 (Escape to Host). Even with shared document roots, traversal controls reduce the exploitable surface area.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Apache configuration for FollowSymLinks and SymLinksIfOwnerMatch options across all Directory blocks to determine if symlink following is restricted.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing `Options -FollowSymLinks` or absence of `FollowSymLinks` confirm symlink traversal is restricted. Presence of `Options +FollowSymLinks` or `Options Indexes FollowSymLinks` without the minus sign indicates controls are NOT enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect nginx configuration files for the `disable_symlinks` directive within server and location blocks.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: `disable_symlinks on;` or `disable_symlinks if_not_owner;` confirms path traversal controls via symlink restriction. No output or `disable_symlinks off;` means controls are absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Audit rewrite rules in Apache .htaccess files and main config for patterns that could resolve paths outside the document root.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any output containing `../` or encoded equivalents in rewrite targets indicates traversal controls are insufficient or bypassed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform an active path traversal probe against a test endpoint to verify the server rejects or neutralises traversal sequences.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A 400 Bad Request or 403 Forbidden with no `/etc/passwd` content confirms controls are active. A 200 response with file content confirms traversal controls are NOT enabled.

typical_values: true (modern nginx defaults, Apache with explicit -FollowSymLinks)
false (legacy Apache installations with default Options Indexes FollowSymLinks, or misconfigured rewrites)

option_description: Indicates whether any TLS private key file path configured in the web server (e.g., Apache SSLCertificateKeyFile or nginx ssl_certificate_key) resolves to a path that is a subdirectory of or equal to the web server's document root, making the private key directly retrievable via an HTTP GET request by any client.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the `private_key_file_exposure` exposure when `input.key_file_in_document_root == true`. If a private key is web-accessible, an unauthenticated remote attacker can retrieve it with a single HTTP request, enabling impersonation of the server, decryption of captured TLS sessions, and complete compromise of the server's PKI trust. This maps to MITRE T1552.004 (Private Keys) and T1552 (Unsecured Credentials) and is rated high criticality with score 8.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract TLS key file paths and document root paths from Apache configuration, then compare canonical paths to determine if any key resides under any document root.
how_to_obtain.command: DOCROOTS=$(grep -rih 'DocumentRoot' /etc/apache2/ /etc/httpd/ 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $2}' | xargs -I{} realpath {} 2>/dev/null); KEYFILES=$(grep -rih 'SSLCertificateKeyFile' /etc/apache2/ /etc/httpd/ 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $2}' | xargs -I{} realpath {} 2>/dev/null); for K in $KEYFILES; do for D in $DOCROOTS; do echo "$K" | grep -q "^$D" && echo "KEY IN DOCROOT: $K under $D"; done; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any line beginning with `KEY IN DOCROOT:` confirms key_file_in_document_root is true. No output confirms keys are stored outside document roots.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract nginx ssl_certificate_key paths and root directives, resolve them, and check for path prefix overlap.
how_to_obtain.command: DOCROOTS=$(nginx -T 2>/dev/null | grep -E '^\s*root ' | awk '{print $2}' | sed 's/;//' | xargs -I{} realpath {} 2>/dev/null); KEYFILES=$(nginx -T 2>/dev/null | grep 'ssl_certificate_key' | awk '{print $2}' | sed 's/;//' | xargs -I{} realpath {} 2>/dev/null); for K in $KEYFILES; do for D in $DOCROOTS; do echo "$K" | grep -q "^$D" && echo "KEY IN DOCROOT: $K under $D"; done; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output showing `KEY IN DOCROOT:` confirms a dangerous key placement. No output is the expected secure state.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Manually inspect TLS key file directives and compare against document root paths in configuration files.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Key file paths such as `/etc/ssl/private/server.key` or `/etc/pki/tls/private/` are secure. Paths under `/var/www/`, `/srv/www/`, or `/usr/share/nginx/html/` are unsafe and set this attribute to true.

typical_values: true (misconfigured deployments where keys are placed alongside certificate files in document-accessible directories, or Let's Encrypt webroot setups where the .well-known path is near key storage)

option_description: Indicates whether the TLS private key file(s) configured for the web server have filesystem permissions that permit reading by OS users outside the owning user or the designated web server service group. Specifically, this flags permissions where the 'others' permission bits include read (o+r), or where the group-read bit is set for a group broader than the dedicated web server group (e.g., mode 644, 666, 777, or 640 with a world-group).
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `private_key_file_exposure` when `input.key_file_world_readable == true`. World-readable private keys allow any local OS user, unprivileged process, or attacker with shell access to read and exfiltrate the private key without root privileges. This enables server impersonation, decryption of historical TLS traffic, and man-in-the-middle attacks. Mapped to MITRE T1552.004 (Private Keys) and T1552 (Unsecured Credentials), rated high criticality score 8.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Locate all TLS private key file paths from Apache and nginx configuration, then check their filesystem permissions using stat to identify world-readable or overly permissive modes.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rih 'SSLCertificateKeyFile\|ssl_certificate_key' /etc/apache2/ /etc/httpd/ /etc/nginx/ 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $NF}' | sed 's/;//' | sort -u | xargs -I{} stat -c '%a %n %U %G' {} 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Permissions of 600 or 640 (with a trusted group) are acceptable. Any mode ending in a non-zero others digit (e.g., 644, 664, 666, 777) or group-readable with a broad group confirms key_file_world_readable is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use find with permission filters to detect any private key files under common TLS directories that have world-readable or group-readable bits set.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Files showing `---------- ` or `-rw-------` (600) or `-rw-r-----` (640) with a privileged group are secure. Files showing `-rw-r--r--` (644), `-rwxr-xr-x` (755), or any world-accessible mode confirm world-readable keys.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Directly test the specific key file permission octal value and compare against the threshold for world-readability.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rih 'SSLCertificateKeyFile\|ssl_certificate_key' /etc/apache2/ /etc/httpd/ /etc/nginx/ 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $NF}' | sed 's/;//' | sort -u | while read f; do PERM=$(stat -c '%a' "$f" 2>/dev/null); OTHER=$((PERM % 10)); [ "$OTHER" -ne 0 ] && echo "WORLD-READABLE: $f ($PERM)"; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any line beginning `WORLD-READABLE:` confirms key_file_world_readable is true. No output confirms others bits are zero (not world-readable).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the key provisioning process (e.g., certbot, manual generation, configuration management scripts) to determine if umask or explicit chmod commands are applied when writing private key files, and whether periodic permission audits are scheduled.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Review cron jobs, Ansible playbooks, Terraform provisioners, or certbot deploy hooks for chmod/chown operations on key files. Check /etc/cron.d/, /etc/cron.daily/, and CI/CD pipeline scripts.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Evidence of `chmod 600 <keyfile>` and `chown root:ssl-cert <keyfile>` in provisioning scripts confirms controlled permissions. Absence of explicit permission enforcement in provisioning indicates risk of world-readable keys from default umask values.

typical_values: false (correctly provisioned keys at 600 owned by root, or 640 owned by root with group ssl-cert/www-data)
true (common in manually deployed certificates where umask is 022, resulting in 644 permissions, or automated tools that do not enforce restrictive modes post-write)
